newsitem.title: CHINA: China parliament in rare protest vote over crime.
newsitem.headline: China parliament in rare protest vote over crime.

text.p: China's usually docile parliament expressed open dissatisfaction with the government's battle against crime on Friday when 40 percent of its deputies rejected the top prosecutor's annual report.
Public opinion polls show rising crime is the chief grievance of many Chinese and the usually rubber-stamp National People's Congress echoed popular feeling with its vote at the closing session.

The 2,750 deputies meeting in the cavernous Great Hall of the People voted by secret ballot on a series of government work reports and new laws -- and chose to display the highest level of opposition yet by the body that generally follows the Communist Party line.
Voting on the annual report this week by Procurator General Zhang Siqing, 675 deputies voted against while 390 abstained and 34 chose to cast no vote.

It was the highest proportion of protest votes on record by the National People's Congress -- just a 59.6 percent support rate. Last year, about 27 percent of deputies did not like the procurator's report.

Deputies showed even less support than a vote in 1995 when nearly one-third rejected the government's choice of Jiang Chunyun, a close ally of party chief and state president Jiang Zemin, as a vice premier in charge of the huge agriculture portfolio.
China's parliament has yet to reject outright any legislation or government appointment set before it.
Deputies also showed their dissatisfaction with the work of China's top judge, with 881 -- or nearly one-third -- choosing not to support a separate report by Supreme Court President Ren Jianxin.

In Procurator General Zhang Siqing's report this week, he said prosecutors had boosted the number of arrests by about 17 percent last year, but much remained to be done to rein in a tide of lawbreaking.
Violent crime, narcotics offences and gang and mafia-style criminal activity remained rampant, he said and warned that "hostile foreign forces" were trying to Westernise and split China.
Top judge Ren told deputies that China's much-vaunted anti-graft crusade had netted thousands of officials who had tried to abuse their bureaucratic clout for personal gain.

Many Chinese say top officials use their influence to stay beyond the reach of the law, citing the lack of action against Beijing's former party boss Chen Xitong, who was dismissed in a graft scandal in 1995.

The parliament also approved a motion to create China's largest municipality -- Chongqing in southwestern Sichuan province. It becomes China's fourth municipality, following Beijing, Shanghai and the northern port city of Tianjin.
The sprawling municipality will have a total population of 30.02 million when its rural suburbs are included.
Deputies approved the budget for 1997, although some 10 percent chose not to support it.
The budget revealed a record debt issue and higher defence spending for 1997.
China aims to cut its budget deficit by 7.2 percent to 57.0 billion yuan ($6.87 billion) in 1997 from 61.442 billion last year, Finance Minister Liu Zhongli said last week.

Total revenues were expected to be 839.794 billion yuan ($101.18 billion) this year, an increase of 14 percent, while expenditures were set at 896.794 billion yuan ($108.047 billion), up by 13.3 percent.
However, Liu said China would miss its target of balancing its books by the year 2000.
Western diplomats say the deficit is manageable, equal to about 0.77 percent of estimated total GDP this year and down from 0.99 percent last year.
